analysis.one_liner: Caps fossil fuel emissions and auctions permits, sending the proceeds to Americans as quarterly cash dividends.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final two weeks of the 117th Congress with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to two House committees and died without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies that produce or import oil, coal, or natural gas to buy carbon permits from the federal government for the emissions their fuels cause. The number of permits would shrink each year until 2050, cutting U.S. carbon dioxide emissions 90% below 2015 levels. Every dollar raised would be divided equally among people lawfully living in the United States with a valid Social Security number, paid quarterly and tax-free. It would also add fees on carbon-intensive imports so foreign manufacturers don't gain an advantage, and it would preserve state lawsuits against fossil fuel companies over climate damage.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households receive an equal quarterly dividend funded entirely by the fossil fuel industry's permit purchases. Because the dividend is the same for everyone while wealthier households buy more fuel, most lower- and middle-income households come out ahead financially. Frontline communities near fossil fuel pollution get expanded air-quality monitoring and a guarantee of additional regulation if local pollutants don't fall as fast as carbon dioxide. States, cities, and individuals keep their right to sue fossil fuel companies for climate damage and deception.

how_it_helps.text: Auctions the right to sell oil, coal, and natural gas in the U.S. market, with the permit quantity shrinking to a 90% cut below 2015 emissions by 2050, and distributes all auction proceeds equally to lawful U.S. residents with valid Social Security numbers as tax-free quarterly dividends [S3].

Starts the permit floor at $40 per ton of carbon dioxide and raises it $10 each year, so the burden falls on the companies that produce and import fossil fuels, while anti-hoarding limits block speculation in the permits [S3].

Directs the EPA to monitor co-pollutant air quality in frontline communities disproportionately harmed by fossil fuel pollution and to impose extra measures if those communities' pollution does not fall in step with the carbon targets [S3].

Imposes carbon equivalency fees on carbon-intensive imports like steel, aluminum, and cement, and pays rebates to U.S. exporters of those goods, protecting domestic jobs while the carbon cap raises production costs [S3].
Preserves state and federal lawsuits against fossil fuel companies over climate damage, deception, nuisance, and negligence, so the emissions cap does not shield the industry in court [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that produce or import crude oil, coal, and natural gas would buy permits for every ton of carbon their fuels emit, and those costs would flow into prices for gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity. Households with above-average energy use, and energy-intensive manufacturers, would likely pay more than they receive in dividends, at least until the border adjustments and dividend catch up. Exporters of carbon-intensive goods would be made whole through payments from the Treasury.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, coal, and natural gas producers and importers

drawbacks.text: Fossil fuel costs would rise immediately while dividends arrive a quarter or more later, and prices of gasoline, home heating, and electricity would rise across the board, straining households before their first dividend payment offsets the increase [S3].

Energy-intensive U.S. industries like steel, cement, glass, and chemicals would face higher production costs than foreign competitors until border adjustments and export rebates are administratively set up, which relies on the Secretary identifying affected goods by rule [S3].
Eligibility requires a valid Social Security number and lawful presence, so dividends would exclude some residents even as fuel prices rose for everyone [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most lower- and middle-income households, an equal per-person dividend funded by fossil fuel permit auctions would exceed their added energy costs, and the shrinking cap is a serious emissions-reduction mechanism with real penalties for noncompliance. The honest costs are the near-term price shock on fuels and electricity, the administrative challenge of valuing carbon content for border adjustments, and the exclusion of some residents from dividends. The bill's design directly addresses the biggest historical objection to carbon pricing — that it hits poor households hardest — by recycling 100% of the revenue equally.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors in the last two weeks of the session, referred to two House committees, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Beyer introduced the bill on December 21, 2022, twelve days before the 117th Congress ended [S1].
It drew zero cosponsors, including no Republicans [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees the day it was introduced, and no committee took further action on it [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, coal, and natural gas producers avoided a rising permit fee on their products, and no one else gained from the outcome — the bill died before any committee considered it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel companies avoided the carbon fee

sides.party_line_note: The sole sponsor was a Democrat and all 429 cosponsor slots went unfilled, with no Republican or additional Democratic support, so the bill never had a visible coalition on either side of the aisle.

industries.note: Would buy carbon permits for every ton of emissions from the fuels they sell, with the permit supply shrinking to 90% below 2015 levels by 2050 and a $40-per-ton floor rising $10 yearly. The bill also preserves lawsuits against the industry for climate damage and deception [S3].
Coal mines and coal importers would be covered entities buying permits for every ton their fuel emits, the steepest relative burden among the covered fuels as the cap tightens [S3].

industries.industry: Natural gas producers, processors, and distributors
industries.note: Gas delivery entities and processors would surrender permits against their emissions each April 1, with a penalty three times the auction price for any shortfall [S3].

industries.industry: Carbon-intensive manufacturers (steel, aluminum, cement, glass, chemicals, paper)
industries.note: These industries would pay more for energy like everyone else, but border fees on comparable imports and rebates to exporters are designed to keep them cost-competitive against foreign producers that face no carbon price [S3].
Fuel and electricity prices would rise across the economy, but the equal quarterly dividend would exceed the added costs for most households and would grow as the permit price rises [S3].
